extraction_notes: Only the 2025-26 Program of Studies (43-page PDF, text-based) is available; no 2026-27 edition was found (Phase 1: outdated_only), so the course list may differ from what is offered in 2026-27. Courses tagged '(26/27 School Year)' (AP United States History, Economics, Wildlife Ecology, Astronomy: Stars, Galaxies & Cosmology) and '(25/26 School Year)' (Astronomy: The Solar System) are included, with the tag in offering_note; the catalog also says not every elective runs every year. Graduation requirements are taken from the 2026-27 Student Handbook (grad_requirements_2026-27.pdf, p.21), with the 2025-26 catalog p.3 version appended in raw_text; the catalog adds that science must include one of Foundations, Chemistry or Physics. The handbook was used for graduation requirements only, no courses were taken from it. Expedition: Justice in Focus appears in both English (p.8) and Social Studies electives (p.13, as 'PBL Expedition: Justice in Focus'); kept as one English record. Intro to Journalism, Writing for Stage and Screen: '(9-12)' in the title moved to grade_levels. Catalog drop-cap artifacts in the PDF text were repaired when copying descriptions. Lengths are only filled where the catalog states them (year/semester); the math overview says only that 'most high school courses meet for one semester', so other 1-credit courses are 'unknown'. Grades 6-8 or 7-8 parts of stated ranges (Algebra I Part 1 gr. 8-12, Independent Studies 7-12, Language Lab 6-12, Hands On Minds Engaged 7-9) were trimmed to 9-12 with the printed range in notes. Windham Regional Career Center (CTE, p.43) is mentioned without program names, so no CTE records were made. Special Education courses (Language Lab, Hands On Minds Engaged, Skill Building) are marked special_program. Dual Enrollment and VTVLC online courses (p.41) are one program record each. Hand Woodworking/Traditional Fine Woodworking is listed as one course. Remaining check warnings (Project Bike Tech, Guitar/Ukulele, Online Courses: description not verbatim 16-23%) are false positives: the PDF text layer splits each paragraph's first letter off (e.g. 'T' / 'his class') in both .txt and .raw.txt, so the 6-word phrases around those splits do not match; the descriptions were compared with the PDF text and are verbatim. Page numbers are PDF page markers in phase2/text (printed page number is one lower).

courses.description: How do we read closely, think deeply, write effectively, and communicate clearly? This required 9th-grade English course prepares students for high school-level writing while exploring questions of identity, voice, and power. Students will strengthen writing fundamentals, including vocabulary, punctuation, grammar, and narrative essay structure, and develop habits and organizational skills to transition to high school with confidence. Through a variety of readings and discussions, students will reflect on what shapes their identity—society, peers, family, community, gender, and race—and discover their own voice. Writing will be approached as a multi-step process, including prewriting, drafting, proofreading, self-editing, and revision, fostering thoughtful discussion, personal reflection, and effective communication. Possible texts include The Hate U Give, by Angie Thomas; The Outsiders, by SE Hinton; The 57 Bus, by Dashka Slater; The Body, by Stephen King; short fiction and nonfiction
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-1 Courses (Grades 9-10); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.description: This course examines how systems of power and identity—including racism, sexism, anti-Semitism, homophobia, and classism—shape our school, community, and world, while exploring how literature promotes justice, dignity, and self-discovery. Students will engage with diverse texts including memoirs, graphic novels, plays, poetry, and short stories, and selections from the Facing History curriculum, “Holocaust and Human Behavior.” Themes of justice, resilience, and social change are central to the course, fostering connections across global experiences and perspectives. Possible texts include Night by Elie Wiesel; In the Sea There Are Crocodiles by Fabio Geda; graphic novel selections including Persepolis, Fun Home, They Called Us Enemy, and Maus; various memoirs, anthologies, short stories, and poetry.
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-1 Courses (Grades 9-10); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.description: A true journalistic product has credibility with its audience; it contains facts and can be used for record-keeping; it covers all aspects of the school year, good, bad, happy, or sad; it also strives to include every person in the school. A journalistic approach will teach you skills in business, graphic design, visual communication, writing, photography, and collaborative relationships. These skills will serve you in whatever field you decide to pursue in the future and in producing the school newspaper.
courses.fulfills_text: Level-1 English Credit OR Elective Credit; may be repeated for elective credit

courses.description: In the first half of the course, students will write 10-minute plays–sometimes called bolts of theatrical lightning– that reflect their own ideas and attitudes. To begin, students will read plays and study the craft of playwriting; then, they’ll draft, revise, and polish their own short plays. At the end of the unit, students’ efforts may culminate in staged readings of their plays for an audience. In the second half of the class, students will learn about the elements of screenwriting and create their own screenplay for a short film. First, we’ll study the artistic and technical aspects of movies–we’ll watch a number of short films and clips from longer ones–and we’ll consider the ways in which they tell stories through images and sound. As a culminating activity, students will collaborate with peers to create and screen a short film produced from a student screenplay. Then we’ll invite an audience to attend a screening! Texts may include A Younger Ten: Writing the Ten-Minute Play, Filmmaking for Teens, and a number of published and unpublished short plays and screenplays.
courses.fulfills_text: Level-1 English Credit OR Elective Credit; may be repeated for elective credit

courses.description: This course is intended to be equivalent to a college first-year English course and is designed to fulfill the curricular requirements of the AP English Course Description of the College Board. We will study a broad range of representative works from a variety of genres and periods and build on students’ analytical and interpretive skills. Literature both informs and enriches our lives as it continually calls into question what we think we know about ourselves and our world. Accordingly, students will be expected to examine characters and themselves with the aim of self-knowledge in mind. The course emphasizes close reading of texts, meaningful discussion of texts, ideas, and literary movements, and clear, concise writing of timed and untimed essays. The course is taken for two semesters (both required). The AP Exam in English Literature and Composition, given in May, is required for all students enrolled in AP English.
courses.prerequisites: Minimum grade of 3 in Level-1 courses and teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.description: Students will explore children's literature through a critical lens, examining themes and motifs that are both universal and specific to the genre. Through close reading and analysis of popular children's literature books, students will refine their literary analysis skills and gain a deeper understanding of the genre. In addition, students will engage in creative writing activities that encourage them to think deeply about the role of children's literature in shaping our understanding of the world including creating their own picture book and engaging in independent projects.
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.description: Designed to be a dual enrollment for Vermont State Colleges, students will read and think critically, write effectively, and learn the fundamentals of literary analysis and grammar. We will use essays, stories, and two or more novels to explore various themes – as students build skills in communication, critical thinking, and research. Students will write daily and revise often, in a variety of genres, including satire, reviews, literary analysis, and personal narratives. We will take inspiration from a variety of writers, as students hone their hone their own writing voice. Students will learn how to find and assess effective sources and how to effectively incorporate research. A research paper with 10 sources, including scholarly research, is the final project. Possible texts: Catcher in the Rye; Handmaid’s Tale; others to be determined.
courses.fulfills_text: Level-2 English credit; Dual-Enrollment for VT State Colleges
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.description: Creative writing is a process that takes courage. This class is an opportunity for students to be open to the joys of writing and to be willing to take risks as they try out many types of writing–from poetry, spoken word, and memoir to screenplays and short stories. What makes a good story? What is a poem, and how do we write one? What are the literary tools that writers use? What do we have to learn from other writers? What does your writing voice sound like? What does it mean to read like a writer? What writers inspire you? Students will decide on a format for sharing their writing–perhaps a zine, a blog, or spoken word performance. Texts will include a self-chosen novel, much short fiction, poetry, memoir, and screenplays.
courses.fulfills_text: Level-2 English Credit; may be repeated for Elective Credit
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.description: This interdisciplinary, project-based course empowers students to explore, analyze, and address critical issues in the American criminal justice system. Using an EL Education framework, students will engage in sustained inquiry into mass incarceration, the school-to-prison pipeline, police reform, and systemic inequities, with a focus on real-world applications. Throughout the semester, students will read diverse texts, examine multiple perspectives, and collaborate to develop solutions to systemic problems. The course culminates in an authentic final project: students will create and present policy proposals to local or state stakeholders, using research and persuasive skills to advocate for change. This hands-on approach fosters critical thinking, civic engagement, and the belief that young people have the power to make a difference.
courses.fulfills_text: Level-2 English Credit; *may complete additional work to earn social studies elective credit
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); Also listed in Social Studies Elective Courses (p.13) as 'PBL Expedition: Justice in Focus' (Grades 11-12; 'Social Studies credit; *may complete additional work to earn English elective credit'); same description, one record kept

courses.course_name: Friending, Crushing, and Othering in Literature
courses.description: This course will examine the theme of friendship–and all the complicated relationships–as students develop analytical reading and writing skills. We’ll ask questions about one of the most important relationships we have, using examples from a variety of novels, films, and excerpts from psychology, anthropology, and journalism. We’ll ask questions about the forces that impact friendships, love, and belonging and how these relationships have evolved throughout history.
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.description: This interdisciplinary, project-based course explores the profound impact of war on individuals, societies, and the human condition through the lenses of literature and history. Combining English Literature of War and a social studies elective in Military History, the course examines how writers, historians, and soldiers have captured the complexities of war across time and cultures. Through engaging with novels, memoirs, poetry, historical documents, and films, students will analyze themes of power, sacrifice, resilience, and justice. This course emphasizes critical thinking, historical inquiry, and literary analysis, while fostering collaboration and creativity through project-based learning. Possible texts include Fallen Angels, Things Fall Apart, Where Angels Fear to Tread, Farewell to Arms, View from the Bridge, The Things They Carried, Julius Cesar, Richard III, Slaughter-House Five, Night, Diary of Anne Frank, The Art of War
courses.fulfills_text: Level-2 English Credit; *may complete additonal work to earn social studies elective credit
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.description: How has the world of sports played a role in American society throughout history? What impact do sports have on building communities? What does our participation in sports reveal about the human spirit? Explore the past, present, and future of sports in the United States, and assess the good, bad, and ugly sides of professional sports from the perspectives of players, coaches, and fans. Possible texts include journals, articles, essays, and videos; readings from Sports Illustrated and other news columns; Friday Night Lights by Buzz Bissinger
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

courses.course_name: America and World History in the 19th Century
courses.description: A required course for ninth grade students and a prerequisite to other history courses. This course will focus on historical events that happened both nationally and globally into the 19th century. Including topics such as the French Revolution, Post Napoleonic Europe, the Industrial Revolution, American Civil War, and Imperialism. These events will be looked at through different lenses: geographic, economic, civic and historical. In this course, students will develop research, reading, and writing skills, by completing a major research project. Students will read a variety of materials, including newspaper articles and primary and secondary sources.

courses.course_name: America and World History in the 20th Century
courses.description: This course starts with causes of World War I and goes through the interwar years into World War II. The course continues to cover topics relevant to world history up until the war on terrorism in the early 2000s. Students will learn and develop the skills of inquiry and research. In this class, students strengthen research, critical analysis, writing, reading, and presentation skills.
courses.prerequisites: Previous participation in America and World History in the 19th Century.

courses.description: This rigorous course offers 9th-12th grade students the opportunity to engage in college-level academics early in high school. Replacing both 19th and 20th Century courses, it examines global cultural, economic, political, and social developments from c. 1200 CE to the present. Students will analyze primary and secondary sources, evaluate evidence, contextualize historical events, and craft well-supported historical arguments. All students are expected to take the AP exam, with credit awarded at the end of the second semester. (Description adapted from the College Board)
courses.prerequisites: 9th graders need approval from the course teacher and a recommendation from their 8th-grade teacher. 10th graders have no prerequisites, but highly recommend completing 19th Century Hist before enrolling.

courses.description: This one-semester foundational course will focus on American citizenship and government. The main topics of the class will be the history of the government’s creation and change over time, civic life, and government. Students will investigate the US government’s separation of powers, and the responsibilities of federal, state, and local governments. Promoting civic virtues and enacting democratic principles will also be priorities.
courses.prerequisites: Previous participation in 9th and 10th grade social studies or AP World History

courses.description: AP U.S. History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university U.S. history course. In AP U.S. History students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods from approximately 1491 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical comparisons; and utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course also provides seven themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and the environment; and culture and society. All students will be expected to sit for the AP US History exam in May. This two credit course will replace Civics and count as an elective.
courses.offering_note: 26/27 School Year; scheduled every year (catalog p.2 note 2)

courses.description: Students learn and apply the principles of micro and macro economics to current social issues and their own lives. Topics include the role of scarcity in economics, the Federal Reserve, different economic systems, supply and demand, inflation and unemployment, Gross Domestic Product, fiscal and monetary policy, and the Federal Reserve and inflation. Students will also learn about financial literacy and consumer life skills.
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Elective Courses (Elective Credit, NOT Social Studies)

courses.description: This course focuses on the military history of the United States from World War II until the present. Topics include World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War, the U.S. War on Drugs, and military actions in the Middle East. The emphasis of the class will be on strategy, technology, motivation, and impact of the U.S. military abroad and at home. Students read, research, analyze, discuss, write, and present their views based on facts, principles, and beliefs.
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Elective Courses (Elective Credit, NOT Social Studies)

courses.description: Based on student and teacher interest, controversial issues will be chosen to study. Students will research, determine reliability, identify bias, and describe evidence supporting varied perspectives on issues. Students will be expected to articulate opinions and support perspectives with meaningful and trustworthy evidence. Constitutional law and Supreme Court cases will be studied when applicable to help understand the legal status of each issue.
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Elective Courses (Elective Credit, NOT Social Studies)

courses.description: This class focuses on introducing students to the thinking, vocabulary, and foundational ideas of psychology. The class begins with a look at the six main perspectives of psychology. The class then moves to units focused around nature vs nurture, neuroscience, learning and human behavior, memory, thinking and intelligence, human development, states of consciousness, motivation and emotion, personality, social psychology, disorder and treatment, and happiness. The course focuses on using demonstrations and active learning of the content. Students will do several research presentations and simulations to learn and apply the content.
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Elective Courses (Elective Credit, NOT Social Studies)

courses.description: This course is a combination of applied mathematics, project based learning (PBL), and individual proficiencies. Applied mathematics shows first hand how students can use mathematics to make better decisions and to solve real world challenges. Students work on a project over an extended period of time that engages them in solving a real-world problem. For individual proficiencies students will be assessed with diagnostic tools in order to create a personalized action plan for each student to differentiate instruction, fill individual knowledge gaps and facilitate meaningful progress.

Students participate in student-centered instruction focused on gaining fluency in operations in the Real Number System. Instruction will also be provided in graphing data, identifying and using functions, applying and comparing geometric relationships, and most importantly, recognizing and seeking algebraic expressions and equations to solve problems. Successful completion of this course will allow students and teachers to reevaluate their multi-year plan with regard to meaningful and appropriate courses to follow.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation or multi-year plan for mathematics

courses.description: Discovering Algebra is designed for the student who has learned the basic mathematics and computational procedures from earlier years, but may lack the number sense to use these skills in a meaningful or creative way. These students may not be quite ready for Algebra I Part 1. Students will develop organization, clear thinking, and strategizing, all important prerequisite skills for success in high school mathematics. Topics include: variables, expression, and integers, solving equations, and inequalities, factors, fractions, and exponents, ratios, proportions, and probability, and linear functions. All topics are focused to develop basic equation solving skills. Success in this class would support enrollment in Discovering Geometry or Algebra I Part 1.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation or multi-year plan for mathematics

courses.description: Following the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum, Algebra I part 1 continues to develop number sense, proportional thinking, and fluency with the real number system. It further develops the language and process of the algebra studied in the earlier grades by manipulating more sophisticated expressions and equations. Emphasis is on working with linear functions with one and/or two variables. Students learn the basics of a graphing calculator as part of learning to create, manipulate, solve, and/or graph linear functions and systems. Additionally, the concepts of probability will be extended. Curriculum used is Illustrative Mathematics.
courses.prerequisites: Pre-algebra, teacher recommendation, or middle schooler commitment to accelerate

courses.description: Following the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum, Algebra I part 2 starts with a quick review of linear functions and then develops the rules for exponents in order to engage in factoring and the solution of quadratic functions. Connections are made to those rules and simplifying square roots. Students learn additional solution methods and applications for quadratic functions. Inverse functions are taught and students learn to solve radical equations. Data analysis concepts are extended.

This course is an introduction to the practical aspects of geometry. Students complete a variety of two- and three-dimensional hands-on projects. This practical application prepares students for theoretical concepts and problem-solving in Euclidean Geometry. Topics include the properties of angles, triangles, quadrilaterals, circles and other two-dimensional shapes, area, perimeter, volume, ratio and proportion, geometric construction, and right angle trigonometry. The text used is Discovering Geometry: An Intuitive Approach (Key Curriculum).
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I Part 1 or Discovering Algebra

courses.description: Students demonstrate high-level reasoning by writing proofs and solving problems dealing with points, lines, angles, triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other shapes. Students study area, perimeter, and volume and the connections between the three dimensions. Students complete a variety of two- and three-dimensional hands-on projects. The texts used are Geometry (Houghton, Mifflin)

This course extends the study of previous algebra courses and assumes a strong working knowledge of those topics. It encompasses the study of functions including logarithmic functions, irrational and complex numbers, polynomial equations, analytic geometry, conic sections, and series and sequences. Concepts in trigonometry are extended to include circular and inverse functions. The text is Algebra II (McDougall, Littell).
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I part 2, Euclidean Geometry or Disc. Geo. with teacher recommendation

courses.description: This course completes the preparation for college-level calculus. Students develop skills in advanced function analysis and the use of these functions for modeling applications. Analytic trigonometry is studied to apply in vector, parametric, and polar applications. Conic sections are reviewed and extended, as are topics in discrete mathematics. Students use graphing calculators on a daily basis.

This course is a broad introduction to the concepts of probability and statistics. Probability consists of collection display, analysis of data, permutations, and combinations. Statistics involves binomial, normal and t-distributions, percentile rank, and standard deviation. Learning objectives include demonstrating statistics encountered in everyday life as well as showing how statistics lend credibility to an argument.

This full-year course prepares students for The College Board Advanced Placement Examination, level AB, which is equivalent to one semester of college calculus. This course includes a brief review of the most important algebraic and transcendental functions and a study of topics in the differential and integral calculus. Students taking this class participate in the AP Calculus exam. Second semester, the course will run every day until the AP Exam in May. The primary text is Calculus: Graphical, Numerical, Algebraic, 3rd ed. (Finney, Demana, Waits, Kennedy).

This course is designed to inform and educate students in concepts of personal finance and money management. Students will begin to develop the skills and strategies that promote personal and financial responsibility related to: financial planning, savings, and investment. Five broad topics will be the foundation of the course: college and/or career planning, money management, savings and investing, income, and spending. There will be several projects incorporated into the curriculum.

This course is a study of the Earth and its place in the universe. Students will explore the origins and geological evolution of Earth, interactions between Earth systems, and the impact of human activities on natural systems, including global climate change. Methods of learning can include hands-on investigations, research reports, projects, and analysis of local and global data.

Students learn to understand the similarities and differences among organisms, genetics, evolution, human anatomy, and physiology. Methods of learning can include fieldwork, laboratory experiments, class discussions, research reports, and self-directed projects. The text is Basic Biology: An Ecological Approach.

This course is designed for any student wanting a solid grounding in chemistry concepts. Students engage in lab experiments regularly. Topics include atomic theory, the periodic table of the elements, properties of matter, types of chemical reactions, and applying chemistry to everyday materials and events. Upperclassmen may earn 4 college credits from Northern Vermont University for successful completion of this course.
courses.fulfills_text: Science credit; May take as 4-credit dual-enrollment class*

courses.description: In this class students will explore how matter and energy interact in the universe. Major topics of study will be motion, forces, energy, momentum & collisions. Students will learn about the physical properties of our universe by engaging in lab investigations and developing mathematical problem-solving skills. Students signing up for this course should be prepared to work outside of class and meet with the teacher as needed to understand challenging material.

Meteorology is the science that deals with the phenomena of the atmosphere, specifically weather and weather conditions. Students investigate how the atmosphere interacts with solar energy to create dynamic weather systems and apply basic meteorological and climatic principles to the study of local, regional and global weather patterns. This course includes an in-depth unit of global climate patterns and changes as well as field trips and guest speakers. Upperclassmen may earn 4 college credits through Northern Vermont University for successful completion of this course.
courses.fulfills_text: Science credit – 4 credit Dual enrollment option

courses.description: This course will examine the geology, weather, wildlife, stream ecology and flora of the Green Mountain State and how all these factors make Vermont, well, Vermont. We will look at the many microclimates of Vermont and how these climates fit into the bigger picture of the Northeast. Comparisons will be drawn from what is occurring in the present day to that of times past. This course will require field work.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth Science and Biology and an understanding of basic algebraic concepts.
courses.notes: Catalog states: Grades 11-12 or permission of the instructor

courses.description: In this course, students will be introduced to the basic concepts of both theoretical and applied chemistry and physics. The goal of this course is to provide a basic foundation in each discipline while focusing on the real-world applications of each. This will be a lecture/lab-based class and will apply for a student’s third required science course for graduation.

In this course, students deepen their understanding of the human body. They compare structures and functions of the musculoskeletal, neurologic, cardiac, respiratory, digestive, renal, immune, endocrine, and reproductive systems. Students apply concepts to real-life situations in health, injury, and disease.

This course is intended to provide an introduction to understanding the science behind crime detection. Course topics are drawn from the fields of chemistry, physics, and biology. The laboratory exercises will include techniques commonly employed in forensic investigations. Examples of topics include fingerprinting, blood splatter analysis, DNA, hair/fiber comparisons, and death investigation. The course will span all ability levels and will be especially valid for those interested in a career in Law Enforcement or Criminal Justice.

Wildlife Ecology will introduce students to ecology and New England wildlife. Topics of study include biodiversity & evolution, ecosystems, species interactions, population dynamics, conservation biology, and state and local ecological issues. Students will be expected to participate in field work. Visits from professionals from a variety of careers in wildlife science will be able to provide insight on career paths and options.

In this course students will explore our solar system and the human endeavors that have allowed us to reach our current levels of understanding. Topics of study include tools & methods of astronomy, night sky observations, the Earth-Sun-Moon system, the solar system, and the search for exoplanets. Students learn by completing activities, labs, projects, and simulated telescope observations. Upperclassmen may earn 4 college credits from Northern Vermont University for successful completion of this course.
courses.fulfills_text: Science credit – 4 credit Dual enrollment option

courses.description: This course is offered every other year, alternating with Astronomy: The Solar System. In this astronomy course, students will focus on the universe beyond our solar system, covering topics such as tools & methods of astronomy, stars, galaxies, cosmology, and the search for extraterrestrial life. Students learn by completing activities, labs, projects, and simulated telescope observations. Upperclassmen may earn 4 college credits from Northern Vermont University for successful completion of this course

This class is designed for students with little to no prior experience in the visual arts. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to both 2D and 3D mediums, allowing students to develop basic knowledge and skills in the world of visual expression. Throughout the semester, students will engage in hands-on activities and projects that explore a variety of artistic techniques. The curriculum is structured to foster creativity, critical thinking, and artistic confidence. Students will learn how to pursue independent projects that align with their artistic interests and goals. Emphasis will be placed on building a strong foundation in fundamental art concepts.

This class is for students who have already completed a beginner-level course or possess equivalent skills and knowledge in the realm of visual arts. This course delves deeper into the exploration of 2D and 3D mediums, challenging students to expand upon their previous experiences and skills. Throughout the semester, students will engage in advanced projects and activities that push the boundaries of traditional artistic techniques. Students will explore independent projects based on their artistic interests and goals. The curriculum is designed to foster a greater depth of understanding, creativity, and mastery in the field of visual expression.
courses.prerequisites: Art & Design 101 or any other art class. May be repeated

courses.description: Students wishing to create a portfolio for consideration in the AP Studio Art examination and possibly earn college credit enroll in this course. The portfolio exam consists of three sections, breadth, quality, and concentration. This program provides the opportunity to earn college-credit and/or advanced placement in college. Those enrolling in this course should plan to work all year on their art, including time outside of school and the summer prior to the beginning of the course.
courses.prerequisites: Foundations of Art, Ceramics and Sculpture, or Painting Exploration and teacher recommendation
courses.offering_note: AP Art and Chinese are held with sufficient enrollment; otherwise students may enroll as independent studies (catalog p.2 note 2)

courses.description: Beginning with basic tools of imagination, pencil, and paper, students will draw, script, and storyboard their ideas, which will then be used to create a 2D animation. With an introduction to photography, using tools in Adobe Photoshop, students will garner a basic understanding of composition and photo manipulation. Building on the previous lessons, students will then learn about and use Non-Linear editing tools found in Adobe Premiere Pro, WeVideo, and personal devices. Students will then be prepared to create and refine their ideas into completed projects. The class will also examine the impact of film and animation and the subtle and not-so-subtle ways it affects American culture.
courses.fulfills_text: Fulfills the Fine Arts credit requirement

courses.description: This course builds from the Video and Animation course and involves working with more advanced software programs such as Studio-Max and Autodesk Maya. Three-dimensional design software provides modeling, animation, simulation, and rendering for motion graphics artists. Students complete short animations for films or games. This is an opportunity to meet the demands of a professional artist.
courses.prerequisites: Video and Animation or permission of the teacher
courses.fulfills_text: Fulfills the Fine Arts credit requirement

courses.description: This hands-on course for 9th through 12th graders empowers students to pursue their project ideas, fostering engagement with the content. Through individual projects, students develop practical skills in storytelling, documenting their project journey, and utilizing Design Thinking and Systems Thinking methodologies to address real-world problems. Emphasis is placed on communication skills, with students learning to convey their project experiences and outcomes through various media effectively. Opportunities for collaboration with outside organizations provide authentic learning experiences, while assessments are based on communication standards aligned with transferable skills. Students are expected to demonstrate curiosity, an exploratory mindset, and perseverance. By participating in this course, students enhance their presentation and storytelling skills, develop project-specific skills, and gain a deeper understanding of Design Thinking and Systems Thinking methodologies.

Project Bike Tech offers an immersive experience in bicycle mechanics, technology, and entrepreneurial skills. In this dynamic course, students not only learn the ins and outs of bicycle maintenance and repair but also gain invaluable insights into running a business and mastering shopcraft. Students delve into the fundamentals of bicycle mechanics, from diagnosing common issues to mastering advanced repair techniques. Through hands-on workshops and classroom instruction, participants gain confidence in using specialized tools and equipment to keep bicycles in top condition. Through simulated business scenarios and real-world projects, students learn how to manage inventory, provide excellent customer service, and market their services effectively. They also develop proficiency in honing their craftsmanship and attention to detail as they customize and refurbish bicycles to meet customer needs. By combining practical skills with business savvy, Project Bike Tech empowers students to not only excel in the bicycle industry but also make a positive impact in their communities. Join us on this exciting journey of discovery, creativity, and entrepreneurship through the world of bicycles!
courses.fulfills_text: Elective credit; students may repeat this course for elective credit

courses.description: Band is for students with at least one year of experience on a band instrument who meet the school band entry requirements. Participants perform in two annual concerts, solo festivals, chamber ensembles, and pep band at varsity basketball games. Instruments can be rented locally. Students also attend 20-minute rotating private lessons throughout the year.

Students study and perform choral music from various periods and cultures, focusing on singing techniques and music reading. They perform in at least two school concerts annually and participate in community events. Students also attend 20-minute rotating private lessons throughout the year.

This class provides instruction in playing technique, chord charts, sheet music, tablature, tuning, and composition. Students learn to play both guitar and ukulele. Depending on the experience levels of enrolled students, the class may be divided into beginner and intermediate/advanced sections.

This course introduces students to the fundamentals of hand tool woodworking, from understanding wood as a resource and developing skills to creating designs and scale drawings for self-directed projects. It also includes antique restoration, where students repair and restore 19th and early 20th-century furniture, focusing on structural issues, veneer repair, and cosmetic restoration. No prior experience is required, and students may repeat the course for additional credit with more challenging projects.

This program is for students serious about woodworking, offering nearly 1000 hours of instruction and self-directed work. Students learn joinery, furniture construction and repair, and antique restoration. Students will keep a detailed journal of their skills, and upon completion, students will have a strong foundation in hand tool use, a portfolio of crafted pieces, a juried exhibition, and a Fine Woodworking Apprenticeship certificate of completion.

Chinese I introduces the language and culture, focusing on listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students learn the Pinyin system, intonation, Chinese writing with strokes and radicals, and typing for digital communication. Cultural activities enhance language learning and awareness, while characters, vocabulary, and grammar are taught through communicative contexts.

Chinese II builds on the four language skills—listening, speaking, reading, and writing—for effective communication. Students expand their knowledge of Chinese characters, grammar, and culture while practicing comprehension, speaking drills, and writing short essays. They also explore proverbs and idioms through basic stories.

Chinese III advances students' skills in listening, speaking, reading, and writing. They practice immersive listening and engage with authentic materials like movies, books, and posters to deepen cultural understanding and language proficiency. Students also explore Chinese literature through reading books, articles, and poems.

Chinese IV is the advanced level of the Chinese language and culture study. The course is intended to further develop the four communication skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing with advanced grammar. This comprehensive curriculum is implemented in an immersion environment where students are encouraged to speak only Chinese in class to ensure and enhance their learning effectiveness. Students will participate in a variety of speaking and writing activities.

This year-long AP course, equivalent to a college sophomore class, develops advanced listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills aligned with the five goals: communication, cultures, connections, comparisons, and communities. Students engage with diverse materials like signs, advertisements, books, films, and contemporary texts from Chinese-speaking communities. Cultural elements are integrated to deepen understanding of China's national and international issues, daily life, and more.
courses.offering_note: AP Art and Chinese are held with sufficient enrollment; otherwise students may enroll as independent studies (catalog p.2 note 2)

courses.description: In Spanish I, students learn the basics of speaking, listening, reading, and writing. They focus on grammar, including present tense verbs, sentence structure, and formal vs. informal language. Vocabulary development enhances speaking, comprehension, and understanding of Latin roots in English and Spanish. By the end of the course, students can discuss functional topics such as greetings, dates, food, sports, school, and family.

Spanish II builds on communication skills, expanding speaking, listening, reading, and writing abilities. Students study vocabulary related to household items, clothing, technology, and leisure activities. They learn grammar, including regular and irregular preterite tense, stem-changing verbs, present progressive, imperative, and object pronouns, enabling them to express opinions, share information, and narrate in Spanish with increased confidence.

Spanish III intensifies linguistic challenges, with more classroom time conducted in Spanish. Students engage in tasks like asking for directions, describing daily routines, and discussing past events. They study reflexive verbs, preterite, imperfect, imperfect progressive, and reciprocal verbs, along with pronouns and possessive adjectives. Reading stories, news articles, and vocabulary exercises enhance language use. Cultural exploration and linguistic development culminate in presentations in various formats, including spoken, written, and artistic.

In this advanced Spanish class, students continue building on previous years of study with a focus on complex grammar, including present perfect, impersonal expressions, imperative, future and conditional tenses, and subjunctive forms. These structures are applied in tasks like expressing opinions, concerns, recommendations, and wishes. Students engage in spoken and written narratives about past, present, and future events, further refining their linguistic, cultural, and vocabulary skills while taking greater responsibility for their mastery of Spanish.

This course is designed to prepare students for taking the Advanced Placement Exam administered by the College Board in May. Students attain an advanced level of fluency in Spanish through an integration of speaking, listening, reading, and writing while performing multiple linguistic and analytical tasks. This course parallels the rigor and commitment of a third-year college level course, and is conducted entirely in Spanish. Course materials include AP Spanish exam texts, listening exercises, and workbook activities and practice tests.

All freshmen must take the Fitness Foundation course as part of their two-credit requirement. This course develops physically literate individuals with the knowledge and confidence for lifelong healthy activity. Students assess their fitness, set S.M.A.R.T. goals, and create a personal fitness plan. Activities include jogging, hiking, yoga, Pilates, shadow boxing, and more, with options often chosen by students. IHT heart rate technology tracks progress, and students use the PLT4M online program to design and implement fitness plans.

This course is an extension of Fitness Foundation and focuses on students’ increased knowledge of how to care for their wellness. Topics covered include nutrition and stress management education. Students will become physically literate individuals who value physical activity and its contributions to a healthy lifestyle. Project-based work will include developing a personalized plan and working to achieve their S.M.A.R.T. goals. Students will have a choice in how to achieve their goals through options such as mountain biking, snowshoeing, hiking, basketball, yoga, resistance training, walk/jog/run, volleyball, and racquet sports. Students will also have access to an online program, PLT4M, which helps design programs for use in the classroom.

Want to get stronger or improve muscular endurance? The weight training curriculum teaches proper lifting techniques, strength training principles, safety, muscle anatomy, and relevant terminology. Students will learn to design and implement their own programs and participate daily to achieve their goals. Access to the online program PLT4M is also provided.

Do you like to participate in adventurous activities? Are you willing to push yourself out of your comfort zone? Do you see yourself as having leadership qualities? The focus of this class will be to develop and train leaders to assist with the use of the High/Low Ropes Course. Students will explore the qualities of a good leader, and work on developing their own leadership skills with the opportunity to become proficient at leading and participating in all the challenges of a low and high ropes course from group initiatives, team building, cooperation, and healthy risk-taking activities.
Students wishing to participate in this must fill out a form with the athletic department!
courses.credits_text: (¼ per season) up to ½ credit

courses.description: This comprehensive course empowers students lead healthy, balanced lives. Topics include effective communication, building positive relationships, and understanding the complexities of mental health. Students will also explore evidence-based sex education and substance education, focusing on making informed decisions and practicing harm reduction and safety. This is an activity and open discussion based class, and students should come prepared to engage and participate. Becoming CPR certified is also an option during this class.

This life skill course introduces students to the complex decision-making skills necessary for the driving environment. It teaches how healthy choices support learners in achieving a lifetime of collision-free driving. Per the VT AOE and the VT DMV, the course requires at least 30 hours of classroom instruction and at least 6 hours of in-vehicle operation, and 6 hours of in-vehicle observation. The in-vehicle course component may necessitate driving after school. Practice driving with a parent or guardian is required throughout the course. In order to be eligible for Driver’s Education, Students must pass all classes in the preceding semester.
courses.prerequisites: VT Driver’s permit and Completed Driver Education Request Form

courses.description: This course connects classroom learning to experience in a workplace setting. Students will design a field study that meets their personal and professional goals. Students will explore career interests and real-world experiences through workplace internships and in-class planning, research, projects, and presentations. Leland and Gray’s Independent Study Program gives students the chance to earn credit in subjects not offered in the regular curriculum. This is a great opportunity to explore personal interests and passions while being supported by a licensed teacher. Independent studies can take place during the school year or over the summer. Students can earn elective credit or credit in a specific subject if a certified teacher agrees to guide the study. All credits count toward Leland & Gray High School graduation requirements.

D.U.O. stands for “Do unto others.” Participants engage in assisting Leland and Gray staff, or tutoring peers. Students can design their own DUO activity during or beyond the school day. Students may earn credit in DUO by fulfilling independent studies requirements. Community Service will be granted

courses.course_name: Journey Away Semester - Land, Food & Culture
courses.description: Spend the semester looking at the ways in which we rely upon the land. Explore food systems, commodities, land based tourism, wilderness skills through an experiential and project based curriculum. After taking a deep dive into ways the landscape influences our lives here in Vermont, we will spend six weeks traveling outside the state exploring ways in which other cultures and communities build and sustain their lives in tandem with the natural world. Will include domestic and international travel.

Senior Survival guides students through the transition from high school to adulthood. Modules include orientation, career exploration, professionalism, job applications, resume writing, cover letters, mock interviews and informational interviews. Students will learn specific skills and strategies as well as transferable skills. Senior Survival is embedded within the Financial Literacy course. Senior Survival will meet once per week during each semester, Through collaborations with faculty and community members, this will be a true community effort resulting in a comprehensive look at how to be prepared for life as an adult. This course IS required for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: This course IS required for graduation.

courses.description: Based on diagnostic assessments resulting in prescriptive instruction in reading and writing, IEP goals and objectives are created to address targeted students’ significant deficits and gaps in the various basic skills areas. Students are assigned to the appropriate lab(s) where they receive specialized instruction. Depending on the need, instruction is either 1:1 or in a small group with a special education teacher. For some high school students, these labs may be used for content area credit through a multi-year plan/personal learning plan.
courses.fulfills_text: Elective credit (may be tied into Skill Building credit)

courses.description: This yearlong special education program for Middle and High school students meets daily for four periods/2 Blocks. Using the student’s IEP as a guideline, students develop practical life long skills based on projects, service-learning activities, and expedition planning and execution. The skill of boat building has been a theme of past projects, such as kayaks of plank on frame, stitch and glue, skin on frame, and cedar strip construction. Using the Circle of Courage model, Special Education students learn to cooperate as a team, develop strong work ethics, and learn the value and satisfaction of volunteer service to the community. Students are placed in this course by their IEP Teams.

Skill building focuses on study skills, time management, organization, reading and writing strategies, group work, communication, transferable skills, and self-advocacy. Students work on the goals of their individual learning plans and Personal Learning Plans.

courses.course_name: Dual Enrollment - College Credit for L&G Courses
courses.description: In 2013, the Vermont Legislature adopted Act 77 - Flexible Pathways in order to allow for greater individualization of secondary school programs as well as to provide opportunities for students to earn college credit while in high school. The Dual Enrollment Program includes college courses offered on a campus of an accredited post-secondary institution and college courses offered by an accredited post-secondary institution on the campus of a secondary school (which can include online courses). Dual enrollment offers eligible students the opportunity to experience college-level classes, take coursework not offered at their schools, and explore possible pathways to their post-secondary futures. Students who successfully complete a dual enrollment course also earn both secondary and college credits. Vermont colleges approved for providing dual credit courses include: VT State University, Landmark College, Community College of Vermont, College of St. Joseph, SIT Graduate Institute, University of Vermont, Norwich University,Bennington College,and Champlain College. Students in grades 11 and 12 are eligible for two vouchers to pay for the course costs. Vouchers can be requested at https://dualenrollment.vermont.gov/vtde. If a student is in the 10th grade or has used both vouchers, they may take additional courses, but may have to pay the course fee out of pocket. LGUHS may also have funds available to cover the course cost. For additional information regarding Dual Enrollment courses at L&G, please contact Terry Davison Berger.
courses.provider: Vermont colleges approved for dual credit

courses.description: Leland and Gray is a member of the Vermont Virtual Online Collaborative (vtvlc.org). As such, students have access to an unlimited amount of online work through VTVLC provided it fits school requirements and space permitting. Visit www.vtvlc.org for more information.
